### RBLS Theorem: Rao-Blackwell-Lehmann-Scheff\mathit{\acute{e}}

If ( \check{\theta} ) is an unbiased estimator of ( \theta ) and ( T(x) ) is a sufficient statistic for ( \theta ), then ( \hat{\theta} = E[\check{\theta} | T(x)] ) is:

1. Valid estimator for ( \theta ) (independent of ( \theta )).
2. Unbiased.
3. Of lesser or equal variance than that of ( \check{\theta} ) for all ( \theta ).

Additionally: If the sufficient statistic is complete, then ( \hat{\theta} ) is MVUE.

### Postulate (1)

( \hat{\theta} = E[\check{\theta} | T(x)] = \int \check{\theta}(x) p(x|T(x); \theta) dx )

Given ( T(x) ) is S.S. (Sufficient Statistic):
( p(x|T(x); \theta) \rightarrow p(x|T(x)) \rightarrow \text{independent of } \theta. )

( p(x|T(x); \theta) \rightarrow p(x|T(x)) \rightarrow \text{independent of } \theta. )

( \hat{\theta} = \int \check{\theta}(x) p(x|T(x)) dx \rightarrow \text{independent of } \theta. )
( = g(T(x)). )

( P(1) \text{ is verified} )

---

### Postulate (2): Is ( \hat{\theta} ) unbiased?

( E[\hat{\theta}] = E[E(\check{\theta}|T(x))] )

( E_1 \rightarrow p(x|T(x)) )
( E_2 \rightarrow p(T(x); \theta) )

( = \int \int \check{\theta}(x) p(x|T(x); \theta) dx \, p(T(x); \theta) dT )

( = \int \check{\theta}(x) \int p(x|T(x); \theta) p(T(x); \theta) dT \, dx )

( = \int \check{\theta}(x) \int p(x, T(x); \theta) dT \, dx )

( = \int \check{\theta}(x) p(x; \theta) dx )

( = E[\check{\theta}] = \theta \rightarrow \text{Unbiased} )

( \hat{\theta} \rightarrow \text{unbiased.} )

### Postulate (3): ( Var(\hat{\theta}) \leq Var(\check{\theta}) )

( Var(\check{\theta}) = E[(\check{\theta} - E(\check{\theta}))^2] )
( = E[(\check{\theta} - \hat{\theta} + \hat{\theta} - E(\check{\theta}))^2] )
( = E[(\check{\theta} - \hat{\theta})^2] + 2 E[(\check{\theta} - \hat{\theta})(\hat{\theta} - E(\check{\theta}))] + E[(\hat{\theta} - E(\check{\theta}))^2] )

Cross-term analysis:
( E[(\check{\theta} - \hat{\theta})(\hat{\theta} - \theta)] = E[(\check{\theta} - \hat{\theta})] \cdot E[(\hat{\theta} - \theta)] \rightarrow 0. )

Using iterated expectations:
( E[(\check{\theta} - \hat{\theta})(\hat{\theta} - \theta)] = E_T E_{\check{\theta}/T} [(\check{\theta} - \hat{\theta})(\hat{\theta} - \theta)] )
( = E_T [(\hat{\theta} - \theta) E_{\check{\theta}/T} (\check{\theta} - \hat{\theta})] \rightarrow 0. )

Since ( E_{\check{\theta}/T}(\check{\theta}) = \hat{\theta} ) and ( E_{\check{\theta}/T}(\hat{\theta}) = \hat{\theta} )

( Var(\check{\theta}) = E[(\check{\theta} - \hat{\theta})^2] + Var(\hat{\theta}) )

As ( E[(\check{\theta} - \hat{\theta})^2] \geq 0 ):
( Var(\check{\theta}) \geq Var(\hat{\theta}) \rightarrow P(3) \text{ is verified.} )

( Var(\check{\theta}) \geq Var(\hat{\theta}) \rightarrow P(3) \text{ is verified.} )

---

### Completeness of a sufficient statistic

Consider the model:
( x(n) = A + w(n) \quad n=0,\dots,N-1 )
( T = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x(n) \leftarrow \text{N.F. factorization} )

( T \rightarrow \text{Complete} \quad E[g(T)] = A \quad \text{--- (1)} )
( g(\cdot) \text{ is the only function for which (1) is true.} )
( g(u) = \frac{u}{N} )

---

### In-complete Sufficient Statistic

Consider the model:
( x(0) = A + w(0) \quad w(0) \sim U\left[-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right] )
( x(0) \sim U\left[A - \frac{1}{2}, A + \frac{1}{2}\right] )

Unbiased estimator of ( A ) is:
( \hat{A} = x(0) )

Have S.S. (Sufficient Statistic) ( T = x(0) ).
( g(T) = T, \quad E(T) = A. )

Challenge: RBLS states ( g(T) ) should be unique for ( T ) to be complete.

Propose that ( E[h(T)] = A. )

Verification:
( v(T) = g(T) - h(T) )

( E(v(T)) = 0 )
( \int v(T) p(T) dT = 0 )

( p(T) \rightarrow \text{pdf of } T, \quad T = x(0) )
( p(T) = \begin{cases} 1 & A - \frac{1}{2} < T < A + \frac{1}{2} \\\\ 0 & \text{elsewhere} \end{cases} )

( \int_{A-\frac{1}{2}}^{A+\frac{1}{2}} v(T) dT = 0 \quad \text{--- (2)} )

( \int_{A-\frac{1}{2}}^{A+\frac{1}{2}} v(T) dT = 0 \quad \text{--- (2)} )

Solution to (2):
( v(T) = \sin 2\pi T )

( \int_{A-\frac{1}{2}}^{A+\frac{1}{2}} \sin 2\pi T dT = \left[ \frac{-\cos 2\pi T}{2\pi} \right]_{A-\frac{1}{2}}^{A+\frac{1}{2}} )

( = \frac{\cos 2\pi(A - \frac{1}{2}) - \cos 2\pi(A + \frac{1}{2})}{2\pi} )

( = \frac{\cos(2\pi A - \pi) - \cos(2\pi A + \pi)}{2\pi} = 0. )

( g(T) - h(T) = \sin 2\pi T. )

( h(T) = g(T) - \sin 2\pi T = T - \sin 2\pi T \neq g(T) \text{ or } T )

( E[h(T)] = A. )

( T \rightarrow \text{incomplete.} )

### Summary

- For a S.S. (Sufficient Statistic) to be complete iff:
( \int v(T) p(T; \theta) dT = 0 \quad \forall \theta )
by only ( v(T) = 0 )

---

### Procedure for Finding MVUE

1. Find the S.S. using N.F. (Neyman-Fisher) factorization: ( \downarrow T(x) )
2. Determine if ( T(x) ) is complete: ( \downarrow )
3. Find a function ( g(T) ) that is unbiased.
4. ( \hat{\theta} = g(T) \rightarrow MVUE. )

---

### Topic: Newton-Raphson for Numerical MLE
When the score function $g(\theta) = \frac{\partial \ln p(x; \theta)}{\partial \theta} = 0$ has no closed-form solution, we use the update rule:
$$\theta_{k+1} = \theta_k - \frac{g(\theta_k)}{g'(\theta_k)}$$
This is derived from the Taylor expansion of $g(\theta)$ around the initial guess $\theta_0$.

pages.text:
( \tan \alpha = \text{slope} = \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} g(\theta) \right|_{\theta=\theta_0} )

( \tan \alpha = \frac{g(\theta) - g(\theta_0)}{\theta - \theta_0} \implies g(\theta) \approx (\theta - \theta_0) \tan \alpha + g(\theta_0) )

Solve ( g(\theta) = 0 ):
( g(\theta_1) = 0. \quad \theta_1 \rightarrow \text{zero of } g(\theta) )

( g(\theta_1) \approx g(\theta_0) + \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} g(\theta) \right|_{\theta=\theta_0} (\theta_1 - \theta_0) )

( \theta_1 - \theta_0 = - \frac{g(\theta_0)}{\left. \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} g(\theta) \right|_{\theta=\theta_0}} )

( \therefore \theta_1 = \theta_0 - \frac{g(\theta_0)}{\left. \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} g(\theta) \right|_{\theta=\theta_0}} )

Iterations: ( \theta_0 \rightarrow \theta_1 \rightarrow \theta_2 ) until convergence

( \theta_{k+1} = \theta_k - \frac{g(\theta_k)}{\left. \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} g(\theta) \right|_{\theta=\theta_k}} )

( \because g(\theta) = \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \ln p(x; \theta) )

( \therefore \theta_{k+1} = \theta_k - [ \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ln p(x; \theta) ]^{-1} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \ln p(x; \theta) )

( \theta_{k+1} = \theta_k - \left( \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ln p(x; \theta) \right)^{-1} \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \ln p(x; \theta) \right|_{\theta=\theta_k} )

( p(x; r) = \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{N/2}} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_n (x(n) - r^n)^2 \right) )

( L(x; r) = \ln p(x; r) = -\frac{N}{2} \ln 2\pi\sigma^2 - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_n (x(n) - r^n)^2 )

( \frac{\partial L}{\partial r} = -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_n 2(x(n) - r^n)(-1) n r^{n-1} = \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sum_n (x(n) - r^n) n r^{n-1} )

( \frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial r^2} = \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sum_n (x(n) n(n-1) r^{n-2} - n(2n-1) r^{2n-2}) )

( = \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sum_n n r^{n-2} ((n-1) x(n) - (2n-1) r^n) )

( r_{k+1} = r_k - \frac{\frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sum_n (x(n) - r^n) n r^{n-1}}{\frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sum_n n r^{n-2} ((n-1) x(n) - (2n-1) r^n)} )

( \hookrightarrow \text{Newton Raphson Method.} )

---

### Scoring Method

Recall ( I(\theta) = -E \left[ \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ln p(x; \theta) \right] )

( \left. \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ln p(x; \theta) \right|_{\theta=\theta_k} \approx -I(\theta_k) )

( \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ln p(x; \theta) = \sum_n \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ln p(x(n); \theta) = N \cdot \left[ \frac{1}{N} \sum_n \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ln p(x(n); \theta) \right] )

### MLE

( L(x, \theta) = -N \ln 2\sigma - \frac{1}{\sigma} \sum_n |x(n) - s(n)| . )

Let ( s(n) = \theta_n . )
Note: ( \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_n} |x(n) - \theta_n| = 1 ) if ( x(n) > \theta_n ) and ( -1 ) if ( x(n) < \theta_n . )

( \implies x(n) - s(n) = 0 )

### 7.21 Example: Normal Distribution with Unknown Mean and Variance

Consider ( x_n \sim N(A, \sigma^2) )

**Estimate ( A ):**
( \frac{\partial L}{\partial A} = 0 \implies \sum_n \frac{2(x(n)-A)}{2\sigma^2} = 0 )
( \implies \hat{A} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_n x(n) )

**Estimate ( \sigma^2 ):**
( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \sigma^2} = 0 \implies -\frac{N}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{1}{2} \frac{(-1)}{(\sigma^2)^2} \sum_n (x(n)-A)^2 = 0 )
( \implies \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{N} \sum_n (x(n)-\hat{A})^2 )

**SNR estimate ( \hat{\eta} ):**
( \hat{\eta} = \frac{(\frac{1}{N} \sum_n x(n))^2}{\frac{1}{N} \sum_n (x(n)-\hat{A})^2} )

**Theorem:** If an efficient estimator exists, then the ML method will produce it.

### Gamma Distribution: Fisher Information Matrix

( pdf: \quad f(x; \alpha, \beta) = \frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)} x^{\alpha-1} e^{-\beta x} )

( x = \{x_n\}_{n=0}^{N-1} \quad N \text{ i.i.d. data given} )

Goal: ( CRBs ) for ( \alpha ) & ( \beta ).

### Fisher Info. Matrix

( I = \begin{bmatrix} I_{11} & I_{12} \\ I_{21} & I_{22} \end{bmatrix} \quad CRB(\theta_i) = [I^{-1}]_{ii} )

( I_{ij} = -E \left[ \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta_i \partial \theta_j} \ln f(x) \right] \quad f = \prod_{n=0}^{N-1} \frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)} x_n^{\alpha-1} e^{-\beta x_n} )

( \ln f = N \alpha \ln \beta - N \ln \Gamma(\alpha) + (\alpha-1) \sum_n \ln x_n - \beta \sum_n x_n )

**Calculation of ( I_{11} ):**
( \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \ln f = N \ln \beta - N \frac{\Gamma'(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)} + \sum_n \ln x_n )
Note: ( \frac{\Gamma'(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)} = \psi(\alpha) ) (digamma function).

( \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \ln f = N \ln \beta - N \psi(\alpha) + \sum_n \ln x_n )

( \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \alpha^2} \ln f = -N \psi'(\alpha) )

( I_{11} = N \psi'(\alpha) )

**Calculation of ( I_{12} ):**
( I_{12} = ? )

( \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta \partial \alpha} \ln f = \frac{N}{\beta} )

( I_{12} = I_{21} = -\frac{N}{\beta} )

### Fisher Information Matrix ( I )

( I = N \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \psi'(\alpha) & -\frac{1}{\beta} \\ -\frac{1}{\beta} & \frac{\alpha}{\beta^2} \end{bmatrix} )

### Inverse Fisher Information Matrix ( I^{-1} )

( I^{-1} = \frac{1}{N} \frac{1}{(\psi'(\alpha) \frac{\alpha}{\beta^2} - \frac{1}{\beta^2})} \begin{bmatrix} \alpha/\beta^2 & 1/\beta \\ 1/\beta & \psi'(\alpha) \end{bmatrix} )

---

### Cramer-Rao Bounds (CRB)

( CRB(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha / \beta^2}{N \beta^2 (\psi'(\alpha) \frac{\alpha}{\beta^2} - \frac{1}{\beta^2})} = \frac{\alpha}{N(\alpha \psi'(\alpha) - 1)} )

( CRB(\beta) = \frac{\psi'(\alpha)}{N(\psi'(\alpha) \frac{\alpha}{\beta^2} - \frac{1}{\beta^2})} = \frac{\psi'(\alpha) \beta^2}{N(\alpha \psi'(\alpha) - 1)} )

( \downarrow )
( \text{Enough data} \quad (\epsilon > 0) )

**Solution:**
( \lim_{N \to \infty} 1 - \text{Pr} \{ |\hat{A} - A| < \epsilon \} )

( = 1 - \lim_{N \to \infty} \text{Pr} \{ -\epsilon < \hat{A} - A < \epsilon \} )

( = 1 - \lim_{N \to \infty} \text{Pr} \{ A - \epsilon < \hat{A} < A + \epsilon \} )

( = 1 - \lim_{N \to \infty} \int_{A-\epsilon}^{A+\epsilon} N(\alpha; A, \frac{\sigma^2}{N}) d\alpha )

Substitute: ( \frac{\alpha - A}{\sqrt{2}\sigma/\sqrt{N}} = \rho \implies d\alpha = d\rho \sqrt{2\sigma^2/N} )

### EM Algorithm: Expectation Maximization

**ML approach (Direct):**
( x \sim p(x; \theta) \rightarrow \text{Access to PDF} )
( \hat{\theta} = \arg \max_{\theta} \ln p(x; \theta) )

**In Practice (Latent Variables):**
( x \sim p(x, z; \theta) )
- ( x ): Observation
- ( z ): Latent / hidden / unobserved variable

**Joint PDF:**
( p(x, z; \theta) = p(x|z; \theta_1) \cdot p(z; \theta_2) )
( \theta = [\theta_1^T, \theta_2^T]^T \rightarrow \text{Unknown} )

( p(x|z; \theta_1) \rightarrow \text{Conditional likelihood} )
- We may know the form, but ( \theta_1 ) is unknown.

( \hat{\theta}_1 = \arg \max_{\theta_1} \ln p(x|z; \theta_1) \quad \rightarrow \text{Not feasible without modification (z is unknown)} )

---

### Sol: EM Algorithm

**E-step (Expectation Step):**
( \ln p(x|z; \theta_1) \longrightarrow E_z [ \ln p(x|z; \theta_1) ] )
- ( p(z) ) is not known completely.

( \ln p(x|z; \theta_1) \longrightarrow \{ f(x), g(z) \} )
( g(z) \rightarrow E[g(z)] \text{ --- moments} )
( E(g(z)) \rightarrow \text{defined in terms of known estimates} )

### EM Algorithm: Iterations and Bayesian Framework

**Iterations:**
( \hat{\theta} \longrightarrow \hat{\theta}_0 \quad \text{Initial values} )
( p(z) \longrightarrow q(z) \quad \text{Approximation} )

( \ln q(z) = \ln p_0(z, \hat{\theta}_2^{(i)}) + \ln p(x|z, \hat{\theta}_1^{(i)}) + \text{const} )
( \uparrow \text{prior} )

**Bayes Law Connection:**
( \text{Posterior} \leftarrow p(z|x) = \frac{p(x, z)}{p(x)} )

( \ln p(z|x) = \underbrace{\ln p_0(z)}_{\hat{\theta}_2} + \underbrace{\ln p(x|z)}_{\hat{\theta}_1 \rightarrow \text{EM estimates}} + \text{const} )
( \downarrow \text{approx.} )
( q(z) \propto p_0(z; \hat{\theta}_2^{(i)}) \cdot p(x|z; \hat{\theta}_1^{(i)}) )

---

### M-step (Maximization)

( E_z [ \ln p(x|z; \theta) ] = \int \ln p(x|z; \theta) q(z) dz )
( \downarrow )
( z, \frac{1}{z}, \ln z \dots \rightarrow \langle z \rangle, \langle \frac{1}{z} \rangle, \dots )
( e_k(z) )

( q(z) \rightarrow p_0(z) \rightarrow \text{Gamma fn.} )

**Parameter Update ( \hat{\theta} \rightarrow ? ):**
( \hat{\theta} = \arg \max_{\theta} E_z [ \ln p(x|z; \theta) ] )

( \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_i} E_z [ \ln p(x|z; \theta) ] = 0 \quad \longrightarrow \text{solve for } \theta_i )

( \begin{cases} \sum_k \pi_k = 1 \\ 0 \le \pi_k \le 1 \end{cases} \implies \pi_k \text{ are probabilities.} )

**Parameters:**
( \theta = [\pi_k, \mu_k, \Sigma_k]_{k=1}^K )
- ( \Sigma_k ): Covariance matrix.

---

### Latent Variable Representation
Introduce a **K-D binary random variable** ( z = [z_1, z_2, \dots, z_K] ).
- **Rule:** Only one ( z_k = 1 ), the rest are all ( 0 ).
- **Example (K=2):** ( z = [1, 0] ) or ( z = [0, 1] ).
- **General:** ( K ) states for ( z ).

**Joint Distribution:**
( p(x, z) = p(z) p(x|z) \quad (\text{Conditional}) )

**Prior Probability of ( z ):**
( p(z_k = 1) = \pi_k )

**Probability of ( z ) (Categorical Definition):**
( p(z) = \prod_{k=1}^K \pi_k^{z_k} \quad \rightarrow \text{def.} )

### EM alg: GM model

( p(x_n, z_n) = \prod_{k=1}^K \pi_k^{z_{nk}} \cdot \prod_{k=1}^K (N(\mu_k, \Sigma_k))^{z_{nk}} )

**Complete data likelihood** ( N - i.i.d, ( x_n ) is D-dim ):
( \Lambda(x, z; \pi, \mu, \Sigma) = \ln \prod_{n=0}^{N-1} p(x_n, z_n) )

( = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{k=1}^K z_{nk} \ln \pi_k + \sum_n \sum_k z_{nk} \left[ \ln \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{D/2}} \frac{1}{|\Sigma_k|^{1/2}} - \frac{1}{2}(x_n - \mu_k)^T \Sigma_k^{-1} (x_n - \mu_k) \right] )

---

### E-step:
( q(z_{nk}) \rightarrow P(z_{nk}=1) )
( \downarrow )
( \gamma_{nk} )

( \hat{\pi}_k, \hat{\mu}_k, \hat{\Sigma}_k \rightarrow \text{initialized} )

( \ln q(z_{nk}) = z_{nk} \cdot [ \ln \pi_k + \ln N(\mu_k, \Sigma_k) ] + \text{const} )
( \exp(\cdot) \rightarrow q(z_{nk}) \propto (\pi_k \cdot N(\mu_k, \Sigma_k))^{z_{nk}} )

**Responsibility ( \gamma_{nk} ):**
( \gamma_{nk} \leftarrow q(z_{nk}) = \frac{\hat{\pi}_k N(\hat{\mu}_k, \hat{\Sigma}_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \hat{\pi}_j N(\hat{\mu}_j, \hat{\Sigma}_j)} \quad \rightarrow \text{Normalizing Const} )

( \langle z_{nk} \rangle = \sum_{z_n} z_{nk} \cdot \gamma_{nk} \quad \bar{z}_n = [z_1=0, z_2=0 \dots z_k=1 \dots z_K=0] )
( \langle z_{nk} \rangle = \gamma_{nk} \quad (j=k) )

### M-step: Estimating ( \pi_k, \mu_k, \Sigma_k )

( \frac{\partial \langle \Lambda \rangle_{q(z)}}{\partial \pi_k} = 0. \quad \langle \Lambda \rangle_{q(z)} = \Lambda \big|_{ \langle z_{nk} \rangle \rightarrow \gamma_{nk} } )

**Constraint Function:** ( \sum_k \pi_k = 1 )

**Lagrange Form:** ( \arg \max_{\pi_k} [ \langle \Lambda \rangle_{q(z)} + \lambda ( \sum_k \pi_k - 1 ) ] )

( \sum_n \gamma_{nk} \cdot \frac{1}{\pi_k} + \lambda = 0. )

Let ( \sum_n \gamma_{nk} = N_k )

( \frac{N_k}{\pi_k} + \lambda = 0 \implies \pi_k = -\frac{N_k}{\lambda} . )

( \sum_k -\frac{N_k}{\lambda} = 1 \therefore \lambda = -\sum_k N_k )

( \pi_k = \frac{N_k}{\sum_k N_k} )

**Verification:**
( \sum_k N_k = \sum_k \sum_n \gamma_{nk} )

( = \sum_k \sum_n \frac{\pi_k N(\mu_k, \Sigma_k)}{\sum_j \pi_j N(\mu_j, \Sigma_j)} )

( = \sum_n \cdot 1 = N. )

( \begin{matrix} N=100. \\ 20\%, 30\%, 50\% \\ N_1, N_2, N_3 \end{matrix} )

( \frac{\partial \langle \Lambda \rangle}{\partial \mu_k} = \sum_n \gamma_{nk} \nabla_{\mu_k} ((x_n - \mu_k)^T \Sigma_k^{-1} (x_n - \mu_k)) = 0 )

( \sum_n \gamma_{nk} (2\Sigma_k^{-1} \mu_k - 2\Sigma_k^{-1} x_n) = 0 )

( \Sigma_k^{-1} (\sum_n \gamma_{nk}) \mu_k = \Sigma_k^{-1} \sum_n \gamma_{nk} x_n )
- ( \text{Matrix} \leftrightarrow \text{Scalar} )
- ( \text{pre-mul } \Sigma_k )

( \therefore \mu_k = \frac{1}{N_k} \sum_n \gamma_{nk} x_n )

---

**M-step: Updating Covariance ( \Sigma_k )**

( \nabla_{\Sigma} \langle \Lambda \rangle = \left. \begin{cases} (+\frac{1}{2}) \sum_n \gamma_{nk} \nabla_{\Sigma} [(x_n - \mu_k)^T \Sigma_k^{-1} (x_n - \mu_k)] \\ -\frac{1}{2} \sum_n \gamma_{nk} \nabla_{\Sigma} \ln |\Sigma_k| \end{cases} \right\} = 0. )

( \text{Tr} \left[ +\frac{1}{2} \sum_n \gamma_{nk} [\Sigma_k^{-1} (x_n - \mu) (x_n - \mu)^T \Sigma_k^{-1}] \right] \quad \text{Tr}((x_n - \mu)(x_n - \mu)^T \Sigma^{-1}) )
( -\frac{1}{2} \sum_n \gamma_{nk} \frac{1}{|\Sigma_k|} \cdot |\Sigma_k| \text{Tr}(\Sigma_k^{-1}) = 0. )

( \implies \sum_n \gamma_{nk} (x_n - \mu_k)(x_n - \mu_k)^T \Sigma_k^{-1} = \sum_n \gamma_{nk} I. )

( \hat{\Sigma}_k = \frac{1}{N_k} \sum_n \gamma_{nk} (x_n - \mu_k)(x_n - \mu_k)^T )

### Least Squares Approach

**System Model:**
( \theta \rightarrow [\text{Signal}] \xrightarrow{s(n)} [\text{Perturbation}] \rightarrow x(n) )
- Perturbation includes **noise** and **model errors**.
- ( x(n) = s(n) + w(n) \quad \longrightarrow \text{What is the model?} )

**Error Model:**
( \theta \rightarrow [\text{Signal}] \xrightarrow{s(n)} (\Sigma) \xrightarrow{e(n)} )
- Obs ( x(n) ) enters at ( (\Sigma) ).
- ( e(n) = x(n) - s(n) \quad \rightarrow \text{error} \quad \rightarrow \text{minimize} )

---

### Least Squares Error
We need to minimize ( f(e(n)) ).

**Formally:**
( \hat{\theta} = \arg \min_{\theta} J(\theta) )
( J(\theta) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (x(n) - s(n))^2 )

**Note:** ( s(n) ) depends on ( \theta ).
**Goal:** Choose ( \theta ) that minimizes ( J(\theta) ).

**Advantages (Args):**
1. Statistical model is not available.
2. MLE is difficult.
3. Optimal estimator is not found.

---

**Example:**
( A \rightarrow [\text{Perturb}] \rightarrow x(n) \quad \implies x(n) = A + w(n) )
( s(n) = A. )
( J(A) = \sum_n (x(n) - A)^2 \quad \longrightarrow \text{Optimization criterion} )

( \arg \min_A J(A) \implies \frac{\partial}{\partial A} J(A) = 0. )
( \sum_n 2(x(n) - A)(-1) = 0 )
( \hat{A} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_n x(n) )

### Linear Least Squares

**Linear assumption:**
( s(n) = \theta h(n) )
- ( \theta ): Unknown parameter.
- ( h(n) ): Known sequence.

**Error criterion:**
( J(\theta) = \sum_n (x(n) - \theta h(n))^2 )

**Optimization (** ( \arg \min_{\theta} J(\theta) ) **):**
( \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} J(\theta) = 0 \implies \sum_n (x(n) - \theta h(n))(-h(n)) = 0 )

( \therefore \hat{\theta} = \frac{\sum_n x(n) h(n)}{\sum_n h^2(n)} \quad [x(n) = H\theta + w(n)] )

**Minimum Error (** ( J_{\min} = J(\hat{\theta}) ) **):**
( J(\hat{\theta}) = \sum_n (x(n) - \hat{\theta} h(n))^2 )
( = \sum_n x(n)(x(n) - \hat{\theta} h(n)) - \hat{\theta} \underbrace{\sum_n (x(n) h(n) - \hat{\theta} h^2(n))}_{S} )

( S = \sum_n (x(n) h(n) - \hat{\theta} h^2(n)) )
( = \sum_n (x(n) h(n) - \frac{\sum_m x(m) h(m)}{\sum_l h^2(l)} h^2(n)) )

### Vector Linear Least Squares Derivation

**Cost Function in Vector Form:**
( J(\theta) = \sum_n (x(n) - s(n))^2 \quad \mathbf{s} = [s(0), s(1), \dots]^T )

( J(\theta) = (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{H}\theta)^T (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{H}\theta) )
( = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{x} - \theta^T\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{H}\theta + \theta^T\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\theta )

**Optimization:**
To find ( \arg \min_{\theta} J(\theta) ), we take the gradient with respect to ( \theta ):

( \nabla_{\theta} J(\theta) = \nabla_{\theta} (\theta^T\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\theta - 2\theta^T\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{x}) = 0 )

( 2\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\theta - 2\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{x} = 0 )

**The Normal Equations / Linear Model Estimator:**
( \hat{\theta} = (\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H})^{-1} \mathbf{H}^T \mathbf{x} \quad \longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} \text{linear} \\ \text{model} \\ \text{estimator} \end{pmatrix} )

### Weighted LS
( J(\theta) = (x - H\theta)^T W (x - H\theta) )

In case of a **diagonal W**:
( J(\theta) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} w_n (x(n) - s(n))^2 \quad w_n = \frac{1}{\sigma_n^2} )

**Role of W:**
1. Enable inversion of ( H^T H \rightarrow H^T W H ).
2. Decorrelation.
3. Diagonal ( W \rightarrow w_n = [W]_{n,n} ) used to emphasize contribution of data samples.

**Sol:** ( \arg \min_{\theta} J(\theta) )

### Goal: Reduce Computation

( \mathbf{H}_{N \times k} \xrightarrow{\text{update}} \mathbf{H}_{N \times (k+1)} )

**Derivation:**
( \hat{\theta}_k \longrightarrow \hat{\theta}_{k+1} )

( \hat{\theta}_k = (\mathbf{H}_k^T \mathbf{H}_k)^{-1} \mathbf{H}_k^T \mathbf{x} \quad J_{\min} = (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{H}_k \hat{\theta}_k)^T (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{H}_k \hat{\theta}_k) )

( \mathbf{H}_{k+1} = [\mathbf{H}_k \quad \mathbf{h}_{k+1}] \longrightarrow [N \times k \quad N \times 1] )

**Example Sequences:**
( \mathbf{H}_1 = [1, 1, \dots, 1]^T )
( \mathbf{H}_2 = [\mathbf{H}_1 \quad \mathbf{h}_2] = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & N-1 \end{bmatrix} \quad \mathbf{h}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 4 \\ \vdots \\ (N-1)^2 \end{bmatrix} )

**Update Rule for ( \hat{\theta}_{k+1} ):**
( \hat{\theta}_{k+1} = \begin{bmatrix} \hat{\theta}_k - \frac{(\mathbf{H}_k^T \mathbf{H}_k)^{-1} \mathbf{H}_k^T \mathbf{h}_{k+1} \mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \mathbf{P}_k^{\perp} \mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \mathbf{P}_k^{\perp} \mathbf{h}_{k+1}} \\\\ \frac{\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \mathbf{P}_k^{\perp} \mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \mathbf{P}_k^{\perp} \mathbf{h}_{k+1}} \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \text{Update} )

---

**Matrix Expansion:**
( \hat{\theta}_{k+1} = (\mathbf{H}_{k+1}^T \mathbf{H}_{k+1})^{-1} \mathbf{H}_{k+1}^T \mathbf{x} )

( = ([\mathbf{H}_k \quad \mathbf{h}_{k+1}]^T [\mathbf{H}_k \quad \mathbf{h}_{k+1}])^{-1} ([\mathbf{H}_k \quad \mathbf{h}_{k+1}])^T \mathbf{x} )

( = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{H}_k^T \mathbf{H}_k & \mathbf{H}_k^T \mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\\\ \mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \mathbf{H}_k & \mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \mathbf{h}_{k+1} \end{pmatrix}^{-1} \longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} k \times k & k \times 1 \\\\ 1 \times k & 1 \times 1 \end{pmatrix} \longrightarrow (k+1) \times (k+1) )

( \mathbf{D}_k = (\mathbf{H}_k^T \mathbf{H}_k)^{-1} )

### Matrix Update Recursion

**Inverse Matrix Update ( \\mathbf{D}_{k+1} ):**

( \\mathbf{D}_{k+1} = \\begin{pmatrix} \\mathbf{D}_k + \\frac{\\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{H}_k \\mathbf{D}_k}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} & -\\frac{\\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} \\\\\\\\ -\\frac{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{H}_k \\mathbf{D}_k}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} & \\frac{1}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} \\end{pmatrix} )

---

**Orthogonal Projection Matrix:**

( \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} = \\mathbf{I} - \\mathbf{H}_k \\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T )

### Recursive Parameter Update ( \\hat{\\theta}_{k+1} )

( \\hat{\\theta}_{k+1} = \\begin{pmatrix} \\mathbf{D}_k + \\frac{\\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{H}_k \\mathbf{D}_k}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} & -\\frac{\\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} \\\\\\\\ -\\frac{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{H}_k \\mathbf{D}_k}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} & \\frac{1}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} \\end{pmatrix} \\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\\\ \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\end{bmatrix} \\mathbf{x} )

( = \\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{x} + \\frac{\\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{H}_k \\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{x}}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} - \\frac{\\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{x}}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} \\\\\\\\ -\\frac{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{H}_k \\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{x}}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} + \\frac{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{x}}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} \\end{bmatrix} )

---

**Simplification using ( \\hat{\\theta}_k ):**

( \\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{x} \\longrightarrow \\hat{\\theta}_k \\quad \\mathbf{D}_k = (\\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{H}_k)^{-1} )

( \\frac{-\\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} ( \\mathbf{I} - \\mathbf{H}_k \\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T ) \\mathbf{x} )

( = \\frac{-\\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{x}}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} \\\\ (k \\times 1) )

### Recursive Minimum Error ( \\mathbf{J}_{min, k+1} )

( J_{min, k+1} = (\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{H}_{k+1} \\hat{\\theta}_{k+1})^T (\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{H}_{k+1} \\hat{\\theta}_{k+1}) )

( = J_{min, k} - \\frac{(\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{x})^2}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} )

**Derivation Expansion:**

( J_{min, k+1} = \\left( \\mathbf{x} - [\\mathbf{H}_k \\quad \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}] \\begin{bmatrix} \\hat{\\theta}_k - \\frac{\\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{x}}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} \\\\\\\\ \\frac{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{x}}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} \\end{bmatrix} \\right)^T \\dots )

( = \\left( \\underbrace{\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{H}_k \\hat{\\theta}_k}_{\\text{Error } e_k} + \\frac{\\mathbf{H}_k \\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{x}}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} - \\frac{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{x}}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} \\right)^T \\dots )

( \\frac{\\mathbf{x}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{H}_k \\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{x}}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} - \\frac{\\mathbf{x}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\underbrace{(\\mathbf{H}_k \\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T)}_{\\mathbf{I}} \\mathbf{H}_k \\hat{\\theta}_k}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} )

( - \\frac{\\mathbf{x}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{x}}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} + \\frac{\\mathbf{x}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{H}_k \\hat{\\theta}_k}{\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}} )

**Fourth Term Expansion:**
( \\frac{\\mathbf{x}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{H}_k \\underbrace{(\\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{H}_k)}_{\\mathbf{I}} \\mathbf{D}_k \\mathbf{H}_k^T \\mathbf{h}_{k+1} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{x}}{(\\mathbf{h}_{k+1}^T \\mathbf{P}_k^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_{k+1})^2} )

### Line Fitting

( s_1(n) = A_1 \\quad s_2(n) = A_2 + B_2 n \\quad n=0, \\dots, N-1 )

**Observation Matrices:**
( \\mathbf{H}_1 = \\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ 1 \\end{bmatrix} \\quad \\mathbf{H}_2 = [\\mathbf{H}_1 \\quad \\mathbf{h}_2] = \\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\\\ 1 & 1 \\\\ \\vdots & \\vdots \\\\ 1 & N-1 \\end{bmatrix} )

**Estimators:**
( \\hat{\\theta} = (\\mathbf{H}^T \\mathbf{H})^{-1} \\mathbf{H}^T \\mathbf{x} )

( \\hat{A}_1 = \\frac{1}{N} \\sum_n x(n) = \\bar{x} )

**Minimum Error for ( s_1 ):**
( J_{min, 1} = (\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{H}_1 \\hat{\\theta}_1)^T (\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{H}_1 \\hat{\\theta}_1) )
( = \\sum_n (x(n) - \\bar{x})^2 \\quad \\longleftarrow (\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{s}_1)^T (\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{s}_1) )

**Update for ( s_2 ):**
( \\hat{\\theta}_2 = \\begin{bmatrix} \\hat{A}_2 \\\\ \\hat{B}_2 \\end{bmatrix} )
( \\hat{\\theta}_2 = \\begin{bmatrix} \\hat{A}_1 \\\\ 0 \\end{bmatrix} + (\\mathbf{H}_2^T \\mathbf{H}_2)^{-1} \\mathbf{h}_2^T (\\mathbf{P}_1^{\\perp} \\mathbf{x}) )

### Recursive Update for Line Fitting ( \\hat{\\theta}_2 )

( \\hat{\\theta}_2 = \\begin{bmatrix} \\hat{\\theta}_1 - \\frac{(\\mathbf{H}_1^T \\mathbf{H}_1)^{-1} \\mathbf{H}_1^T \\mathbf{h}_2 (\\mathbf{h}_2^T \\mathbf{P}_1^{\\perp} \\mathbf{x})}{\\mathbf{h}_2^T \\mathbf{P}_1^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_2} \\\\\\\\ \\frac{\\mathbf{h}_2^T \\mathbf{P}_1^{\\perp} \\mathbf{x}}{\\mathbf{h}_2^T \\mathbf{P}_1^{\\perp} \\mathbf{h}_2} \\end{bmatrix} )

**Component Calculations:**
* ( \\mathbf{H}_1^T \\mathbf{H}_1 = N )
* ( \\mathbf{D}_1 = 1/N )
* ( \\mathbf{P}_1^{\\perp} = \\mathbf{I} - \\mathbf{H}_1 \\mathbf{D}_1 \\mathbf{H}_1^T )

( \\mathbf{P}_1^{\\perp} = \\mathbf{I} - \\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ 1 \\end{bmatrix} \\frac{1}{N} [1, \\dots, 1] = \\mathbf{I} - \\frac{\\mathbf{1} \\mathbf{1}^T}{N} )

**Projection of Data:**
( \\mathbf{P}_1^{\\perp} \\mathbf{x} = (\\mathbf{I} - \\frac{\\mathbf{1} \\mathbf{1}^T}{N}) \\begin{bmatrix} x(0) \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ x(N-1) \\end{bmatrix} = \\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{1} \\bar{x} )

**Projected Sequence Product:**
( \\mathbf{h}_2^T \\mathbf{P}_1^{\\perp} \\mathbf{x} = \\mathbf{h}_2^T (\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{1} \\bar{x}) = [0, 1, \\dots, N-1] \\begin{bmatrix} x(0) - \\bar{x} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ x(N-1) - \\bar{x} \\end{bmatrix} )

( = \\left[ \\sum_n n x(n) - \\bar{x} \\sum_n n \\right] )

( = \\sum_n n x(n) - \\bar{x} \\frac{N(N-1)}{2} )

---

( \\mathbf{H}_1^T \\mathbf{h}_2 = [1, 1, \\dots, 1] \\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\\\ 1 \\\\ \\vdots \\end{bmatrix} \\implies \\sum n = \\frac{N(N-1)}{2} )

( \\text{Denominator } \\longrightarrow \\frac{N(N^2-1)}{12} )

### Sequential Least Squares

**Example: Constant Signal Model**

**Updating for the next sample ( n = N ):**
( \\hat{A}_N = \\frac{1}{N+1} \\sum_{n=0}^{N} x(n) )
( = \\frac{1}{N+1} \\left[ \\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x(n) + x(N) \\right] )
( = \\frac{1}{N+1} [N \\cdot \\hat{A}_{N-1} + x(N)] \\quad \\begin{matrix} \\text{prev. est} \\\\ \\downarrow \\end{matrix} \\quad \\begin{matrix} \\text{most recent data sample} \\\\ \\downarrow \\end{matrix} )

---

### The Sequential Update Structure
( \\hat{A}_N = \\hat{A}_{N-1} + \\frac{1}{N+1} (x(N) - \\hat{A}_{N-1}) )
- ( \\hat{A}_{N-1} \\rightarrow \\text{previous estimate} )
- ( x(N) - \\hat{A}_{N-1} \\rightarrow \\text{prediction error} )
- ( \\frac{1}{N+1} \\rightarrow \\text{correction weight} )

**General Form:**
**New estimate = Current estimate + (Weight)(Error)**

( \\frac{x(N) - \\hat{A}_{N-1}}{N+1} \\longrightarrow \\text{depends on } N )

( \\hat{A}_N = \\hat{A}_{N-1} + \\frac{1}{N+1} e_n \\longrightarrow \\text{if } e_n \\to 0, \\text{ prediction is good.} )

( J_{min, N-1} = \\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (x(n) - \\hat{A}_{N-1})^2 )

**Sequential computation of** ( J_{min, N} = \\sum_{n=0}^{N} (x(n) - \\hat{A}_N)^2 ):

( J_{min, N} = \\sum_{n=0}^{N} (x(n) - \\hat{A}_{N-1} + \\hat{A}_{N-1} - \\hat{A}_N)^2 )

( = \\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (x(n) - \\hat{A}_{N-1})^2 + \\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (\\hat{A}_N - \\hat{A}_{N-1})^2 + 2 \\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (x(n) - \\hat{A}_{N-1})(\\hat{A}_N - \\hat{A}_{N-1}) + (x(N) - \\hat{A}_N)^2 )

( J_{min, N} = J_{min, N-1} + \\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \\left[ \\frac{1}{N+1}(x(N) - \\hat{A}_{N-1}) \\right]^2 + 2 \\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (x(n) - \\hat{A}_{N-1})(\\hat{A}_N - \\hat{A}_{N-1}) + (x(N) - \\hat{A}_N)^2 )

**Simplification of cross-term:**
( 2 (\\hat{A}_N - \\hat{A}_{N-1}) \\underbrace{\\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (x(n) - \\hat{A}_{N-1})}_{0} = 0 )

( J_{min, N} = J_{min, N-1} + N \\cdot \\frac{1}{(N+1)^2} (x(N) - \\hat{A}_{N-1})^2 + (x(N) - \\hat{A}_{N-1} + \\hat{A}_{N-1} - \\hat{A}_N)^2 )

( = \\frac{N}{(N+1)^2} (x(N) - \\hat{A}_{N-1})^2 + (x(N) - \\hat{A}_{N-1})^2 \\left[ 1 + \\frac{1}{(N+1)^2} - \\frac{2}{N+1} \\right] )

### Analysis of the Gain Factor ( \\mathbf{k(N)} )

( k(N) = \\frac{1/\\sigma_N^2}{\\sum_{i=0}^N 1/\\sigma_i^2} )

**Special Cases:**
* **I.I.D. Noise:** If ( \\sigma_N^2 = \\sigma^2 ) for all ( n ), then ( k(N) = \\frac{1}{N+1} ).
* **High Variance at step N:** If ( \\sigma_N^2 \\to \\infty ), then ( k(N) \\to 0 ). The update ignores the noisy new sample.
* **Low Variance at step N:** If ( \\sigma_N^2 \\to 0 ), then ( k(N) \\to 1 ).
  ( \\hat{A}_N = \\hat{A}_{N-1} + 1(x(N) - \\hat{A}_{N-1}) \\approx x(N) ). The estimator trusts the new sample completely.

---

### Variance of the Estimator ( \\text{Var}(\\hat{A}_{N-1}) )

( \\text{Var}(\\hat{A}_{N-1}) = E[\\hat{A}_{N-1}^2] - (E[\\hat{A}_{N-1}])^2 )

( E[\\hat{A}_{N-1}^2] = E \\left[ \\frac{1}{(\\sum \\frac{1}{\\sigma_n^2})^2} \\cdot \\sum_n \\frac{x(n)}{\\sigma_n^2} \\cdot \\sum_m \\frac{x(m)}{\\sigma_m^2} \\right] )

( = \\frac{1}{(\\sum \\frac{1}{\\sigma_n^2})^2} \\sum_n \\sum_m \\frac{1}{\\sigma_n^2 \\sigma_m^2} E[x(n)x(m)] )

Using ( E[x(n)x(m)] = A^2 + \\sigma_n^2 \\delta(n-m) ):

( E[\\hat{A}_{N-1}^2] = \\frac{1}{(\\sum \\frac{1}{\\sigma_n^2})^2} \\sum_n \\sum_m \\frac{1}{\\sigma_n^2 \\sigma_m^2} (A^2 + \\sigma_n^2 \\delta(n-m)) )

( = A^2 + \\frac{\\sum_n \\frac{1}{\\sigma_n^2}}{(\\sum \\frac{1}{\\sigma_n^2})^2} = A^2 + \\frac{1}{\\sum_n \\frac{1}{\\sigma_n^2}} )

### MSE Comparison: Classical vs. Truncated Estimator

To prove that $\operatorname{mse}(\hat{A}) > \operatorname{mse}(\check{A})$, decompose the MSE integral into three regions:

$$
\operatorname{mse}(\hat{A})
=
\int_{-\infty}^{-A_0} (\xi-A)^2 p_{\hat{A}}(\xi;A)\, d\xi
+
\int_{-A_0}^{A_0} (\xi-A)^2 p_{\hat{A}}(\xi;A)\, d\xi
+
\int_{A_0}^{\infty} (\xi-A)^2 p_{\hat{A}}(\xi;A)\, d\xi
$$

Analysis of Region 1 $(\xi \leq -A_0)$:

In this region,

$$
(\xi-A)^2 > (-A_0-A)^2
$$

Hence,

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{-A_0} (\xi-A)^2 p_{\hat{A}}(\xi;A)\, d\xi
>
(-A_0-A)^2
\int_{-\infty}^{-A_0} p_{\hat{A}}(\xi;A)\, d\xi
$$

Using

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{-A_0} p_{\hat{A}}(\xi;A)\, d\xi
=
\Pr\{\bar{x}\leq -A_0\}
$$

we obtain

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{-A_0} (\xi-A)^2 p_{\hat{A}}(\xi;A)\, d\xi
>
(A_0+A)^2\Pr\{\bar{x}\leq -A_0\}
$$

---

Analysis of Region 3 $(\xi \geq A_0)$:

Similarly,

$$
(\xi-A)^2 > (A_0-A)^2
$$

Therefore,

$$
\int_{A_0}^{\infty} (\xi-A)^2 p_{\hat{A}}(\xi;A)\, d\xi
>
(A_0-A)^2
\int_{A_0}^{\infty} p_{\hat{A}}(\xi;A)\, d\xi
$$

Using

$$
\int_{A_0}^{\infty} p_{\hat{A}}(\xi;A)\, d\xi
=
\Pr\{\bar{x}\geq A_0\}
$$

we get

$$
\int_{A_0}^{\infty} (\xi-A)^2 p_{\hat{A}}(\xi;A)\, d\xi
>
(A_0-A)^2\Pr\{\bar{x}\geq A_0\}
$$

Conclusion:

Since the error contributed by the classical estimator in the out-of-bounds regions is larger than the error at the truncation points,

$$
\operatorname{mse}(\hat{A})
>
(-A_0-A)^2\Pr\{\bar{x}\leq -A_0\}
+
\int_{-A_0}^{A_0} (\xi-A)^2 p_{\hat{A}}(\xi;A)\, d\xi
+
(A_0-A)^2\Pr\{\bar{x}\geq A_0\}
$$

Hence,

$$
\operatorname{mse}(\hat{A})
>
\operatorname{mse}(\check{A})
$$

### Final MSE Formulation for the Truncated Estimator

Continuing the derivation for the Mean Square Error of the truncated estimator $\check{A}$:

$$ mse(\check{A}) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (\xi - A)^2 p_{\check{A}}(\xi, A) d\xi $$

Decomposing the integral based on the PDF containing Dirac delta impulses at the boundaries:

$$ = \int_{-\infty}^{-A_0} (\xi - A)^2 Pr\{ \bar{x} \leq -A_0 \} \delta(\xi + A_0) d\xi + \int_{-A_0}^{A_0} (\xi - A)^2 p_{\hat{A}}(\xi) d\xi + \int_{A_0}^{\infty} (\xi - A)^2 Pr\{ \bar{x} \geq A_0 \} \delta(\xi - A_0) d\xi $$

By the sifting property of the impulse function:

$$ mse(\check{A}) = (-A_0 - A)^2 Pr\{ \bar{x} \leq -A_0 \} + \int_{-A_0}^{A_0} (\xi - A)^2 p_{\hat{A}}(\xi) d\xi + (A_0 - A)^2 Pr\{ \bar{x} \geq A_0 \} $$

**Conclusion:**
$$ \therefore mse(\hat{A}) > mse(\check{A}) $$

Thus, $\check{A}$ is a **better estimator** in terms of MSE compared to the classical MVUE $\hat{A}$ when prior knowledge of the parameter range is available.

---

### The "Big" Question

* **Classical MVUE:** Good, but often not enough because it ignores constraints.
* **Prior Knowledge:** If a prior is available, we move from standard MSE to **Bmse (Bayesian Mean Square Error)**.

$$ mse \longrightarrow Bmse \text{ (Bayesian MSE)} $$

pages.text:
### Bayesian Estimation Framework

**Approach:** 
Assume the true parameter $A$ belongs to a known interval, e.g., $A \in [-A_0, A_0]$. In the Bayesian framework, we **randomize** $A$ by treating it as a random variable with a prior probability density function $p(A)$.

**Revised Data Model:**
1.  **Prior Distribution:** A value $A$ is "chosen" from a prior distribution (e.g., a Uniform distribution between $-A_0$ and $A_0$ with height $1/2A_0$).
2.  **Observation:** Noise $w(n)$ is added to the chosen $A$ to produce the data $x(n) = A + w(n)$.



---

### Optimization Criterion: Bayesian MSE (Bmse)

Unlike classical MSE, which is a function of the fixed parameter, **Bmse** is an expectation over both the data $\mathbf{x}$ and the random parameter $A$.

* **Criterion:** $Bmse(\hat{A}) = E[(A - \hat{A})^2]$
* **Integral Form:** $Bmse(\hat{A}) = \iint (A - \hat{A})^2 p(\mathbf{x}, A) d\mathbf{x} dA$
    * Uses the **Joint PDF** $p(\mathbf{x}, A)$.

**Comparison:**
* Classical $mse(\hat{A}) = \int (\hat{A} - A)^2 p(\mathbf{x}; A) d\mathbf{x}$ (Uses the **likelihood**).
* A direct comparison between the two is generally not possible because they operate on different probability spaces.

---

### Bayesian Components and the Posterior

Using Bayes' Rule, the joint PDF is decomposed as:
$$p(\mathbf{x}, A) = p(A|\mathbf{x}) p(\mathbf{x}) = p(\mathbf{x}|A) p(A)$$

* **$p(A|\mathbf{x})$:** Posterior PDF (Our knowledge of $A$ after seeing the data).
* **$p(\mathbf{x})$:** Evidence.
* **$p(\mathbf{x}|A)$:** Likelihood.
* **$p(A)$:** Prior (Our initial knowledge).



**Bmse Minimization:**
$$Bmse(\hat{A}) = \int \left[ \int (A - \hat{A})^2 p(A|\mathbf{x}) dA \right] p(\mathbf{x}) d\mathbf{x}$$

To minimize the total error, we seek the estimator $\hat{A}$ that minimizes the inner integral for every possible observation $\mathbf{x}$:
$$\arg \min_{\hat{A}} Bmse(\hat{A})$$

### Derivation of the MMSE Estimator

To find the estimator $\hat{A}$ that minimizes the **Bayesian Mean Square Error (Bmse)**, we take the derivative of the inner integral with respect to $\hat{A}$ and set it to zero:

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial \hat{A}} \int (A - \hat{A})^2 p(A|\mathbf{x}) dA = 0$$

By differentiating inside the integral:

$$\int 2(A - \hat{A}) p(A|\mathbf{x}) dA = 0$$

$$\hat{A} \underbrace{\int p(A|\mathbf{x}) dA}_{1} = \underbrace{\int A p(A|\mathbf{x}) dA}_{E[A|\mathbf{x}]}$$

$$\therefore \hat{A} = E[A|\mathbf{x}] \longrightarrow \text{Posterior Mean}$$

This proves that the **Minimum Mean Square Error (MMSE)** estimator is the mean of the posterior distribution.

---

### Finding the Posterior using Bayes' Law

To calculate $\hat{A}$, we need the **Posterior PDF** $p(A|\mathbf{x})$:

$$p(A|\mathbf{x}) = \frac{p(A) p(\mathbf{x}|A)}{p(\mathbf{x})} = \frac{p(\mathbf{x}|A) p(A)}{\int p(\mathbf{x}|A) p(A) dA}$$

**Example Case: Gaussian Likelihood with Uniform Prior**
* **Prior:** $p(A) = U[-A_0, A_0]$
* **Model:** $x(n) = A + w(n), \quad n=0, \dots, N-1$
* **Independence:** $w(n)$ and $A$ are independent.
* **Noise:** $w(n) \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$
* **Conditional Likelihood (Single Sample):** $p(x(n)|A) = N(A, \sigma^2)$

**Total Conditional Likelihood:**
Assuming i.i.d. noise samples, the joint likelihood is the product of individual sample likelihoods:

$$p(\mathbf{x}|A) = \prod_{n=0}^{N-1} p(x(n)|A)$$

$$= \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{N/2}} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (x(n) - A)^2 \right)$$

### Computing the Posterior PDF for a Truncated Parameter

Following the Bayesian framework, we combine a **Gaussian Likelihood** with a **Uniform Prior** $p(A) = \frac{1}{2A_0}$ for $|A| \leq A_0$. 

**The Posterior Equation:**
$$p(A|\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{N/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_n (x(n)-A)^2\right) \cdot \frac{1}{2A_0}}{\int_{-A_0}^{A_0} \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{N/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_n (x(n)-A)^2\right) \cdot \frac{1}{2A_0} dA}$$

For $|A| > A_0$, the posterior is $0$.

---

### Simplifying the Exponent
To make the integration manageable, we expand the squared term in the exponent:
$$\sum_n (x(n)-A)^2 = \sum_n x^2(n) + NA^2 - 2A\sum_n x(n)$$
$$= \sum_n x^2(n) + N(A^2 - 2A\bar{x})$$

* The term $\sum x^2(n)$ is a constant with respect to $A$ and cancels out in the ratio of the numerator and denominator.
* We "complete the square" for the remaining terms:
$$N(A^2 - 2A\bar{x}) = N((A-\bar{x})^2 - \bar{x}^2)$$
* The term $\exp\left(\frac{N\bar{x}^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$ also cancels out.

---

### Final Form: The Truncated Gaussian Posterior
The posterior PDF simplifies to a Gaussian distribution centered at the sample mean $\bar{x}$, but restricted to the interval $[-A_0, A_0]$:

$$p(A|\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{C} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2/N}} \exp\left(-\frac{(A-\bar{x})^2}{2\sigma^2/N}\right) & |A| \leq A_0 \\ 0 & |A| > A_0 \end{cases}$$

**The Normalization Constant ($C$):**
$C$ is the area under the Gaussian curve within the prior limits:
$$C = \int_{-A_0}^{A_0} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2/N}} \exp\left(-\frac{(A-\bar{x})^2}{2\sigma^2/N}\right) dA$$

pages.text:
### The Bayesian MMSE Estimator and Computational Challenges

To find the **MMSE (Minimum Mean Square Error)** estimator, we compute the expectation of the parameter $A$ given the data $\mathbf{x}$:

$$E[A|\mathbf{x}] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} A p(A|\mathbf{x}) dA$$

Substituting our truncated Gaussian posterior:

$$E[A|\mathbf{x}] = \int_{-A_0}^{A_0} \frac{A}{C \sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2/N}} \exp\left( -\frac{(A-\bar{x})^2}{2\sigma^2/N} \right) dA$$

**Key Observations:**
* **No Closed Form:** This integral generally does not have a simple algebraic solution because of the truncation limits. 
* **Numerical Methods:** To find a specific value, one must use numerical integration techniques.

---

### Summary of the Bayesian Workflow



**Advantages:**
* The **Posterior PDF** $p(A|\mathbf{x})$ exists for all parameters $A$ and observations $\mathbf{x}$, provided the prior and likelihood are valid.

**Computational Drawbacks:**
1.  **Intractable Denominator:** The evidence term $p(\mathbf{x}) = \int p(\mathbf{x}|\theta) p(\theta) d\theta$ is often difficult to compute, especially in high-dimensional spaces.
2.  **Reliance on Numerical Methods:** Since analytical solutions are rare, we often rely on simulations or approximation methods (like Monte Carlo).
3.  **Expensive Integration:** Calculating $E[\theta|\mathbf{x}] = \int \theta p(\theta|\mathbf{x}) d\theta$ for an $N$-dimensional parameter space ($N$-D) is computationally expensive and slow.

### Example 10.1: Transitioning to a Gaussian Prior

In the previous example, we saw that a **Uniform Prior** leads to a truncated Gaussian posterior with no closed-form solution for the mean. To obtain a **closed-form** solution, we consider a **Gaussian Prior**.

**Prior Knowledge Comparison:**
* **Uniform Prior:** $p(A) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2A_0} & |A| \leq A_0 \\ 0 & |A| > A_0 \end{cases}$
* **Gaussian Prior:** $p(A) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_A^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma_A^2}(A - \mu_A)^2\right)$
    * Which means $p(A) \sim N(\mu_A, \sigma_A^2)$.



---

### The Closed-Form Posterior

With a Gaussian prior and a Gaussian likelihood, the posterior $p(A|\mathbf{x})$ will also be Gaussian. This is because the Gaussian distribution is a **conjugate prior** for the mean of a Gaussian likelihood.

**Likelihood:**
$$p(\mathbf{x}|A) = \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{N/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (x(n) - A)^2\right)$$

**Posterior Calculation:**
$$p(A|\mathbf{x}) \propto p(A) p(\mathbf{x}|A)$$
$$p(A|\mathbf{x}) \propto N(\mu_A, \sigma_A^2) \cdot N(A, \sigma^2/N)$$

By multiplying two Gaussian functions, the result is another Gaussian function. This ensures that the posterior $p(A|\mathbf{x})$ has a **closed-form** analytical solution, allowing us to find the MMSE estimator (the posterior mean) without numerical integration.

### Deriving the Gaussian Posterior PDF

To find the closed-form solution for the posterior $p(A|\mathbf{x})$, we multiply the Gaussian prior and the Gaussian likelihood. We focus on the terms inside the exponent that depend on $A$.

**Exponent Expansion:**
$$p(A|\mathbf{x}) \propto \exp \left[ -\frac{1}{2\sigma_A^2} (A-\mu_A)^2 - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (x(n)-A)^2 \right]$$

Expanding the quadratic terms:
$$p(A|\mathbf{x}) \propto \exp \left[ -\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{A^2 - 2A\mu_A + \mu_A^2}{\sigma_A^2} + \frac{NA^2 - 2A\sum x(n) + \sum x^2(n)}{\sigma^2} \right) \right]$$

**Grouping by Powers of $A$:**
We can rewrite the expression in the standard quadratic form $-(aA^2 + bA + c)$:
$$p(A|\mathbf{x}) = K \cdot \exp \left[ -A^2 \left( \frac{1}{2\sigma_A^2} + \frac{N}{2\sigma^2} \right) + A \left( \frac{\mu_A}{\sigma_A^2} + \frac{N\bar{x}}{\sigma^2} \right) - \left( \frac{\mu_A^2}{2\sigma_A^2} + \frac{\sum x^2(n)}{2\sigma^2} \right) \right]$$

* **$K$:** This constant represents the normalization factor and all terms independent of $A$. In Bayesian derivation, these are often "ignored" until the final step of ensuring the PDF integrates to $1$.
* **The Denominator:** $\int p(\mathbf{x}|A)p(A) dA$ is also independent of $A$ and is absorbed into the constant $K$.

**Standard Gaussian Form:**
The final result is a Gaussian PDF with an updated mean $\mu_{A|\mathbf{x}}$ and updated variance $\sigma_{A|\mathbf{x}}^2$:
$$\therefore p(A|\mathbf{x}) = K \cdot \exp \left\{ -\frac{A^2}{2\sigma_{A|\mathbf{x}}^2} + A \cdot \frac{\mu_{A|\mathbf{x}}}{\sigma_{A|\mathbf{x}}^2} - \frac{\mu_{A|\mathbf{x}}^2}{2\sigma_{A|\mathbf{x}}^2} \right\}$$

pages.text:
### Final Parameter Identification for the Gaussian Posterior

To find the closed-form parameters, we equate the coefficients of $A$ and $A^2$ from our expanded exponent with the standard Gaussian form.

**1. Identifying Posterior Variance ( $\sigma_{A|\mathbf{x}}^2$ ):**
By equating the coefficients of $A^2$:
$$\frac{1}{2\sigma_{A|\mathbf{x}}^2} = \frac{1}{2\sigma_A^2} + \frac{N}{2\sigma^2}$$

$$\Rightarrow \sigma_{A|\mathbf{x}}^2 = \frac{\sigma^2 \sigma_A^2}{\sigma^2 + N\sigma_A^2} \longrightarrow \text{Posterior Variance}$$

---

**2. Identifying Posterior Mean ( $\mu_{A|\mathbf{x}}$ ):**
By equating the coefficients of $A$:
$$\frac{\mu_{A|\mathbf{x}}}{\sigma_{A|\mathbf{x}}^2} = \frac{\mu_A}{\sigma_A^2} + \frac{N\bar{x}}{\sigma^2}$$

Substituting $\sigma_{A|\mathbf{x}}^2$ and simplifying:
$$\mu_{A|\mathbf{x}} = \frac{\sigma^2 \sigma_A^2}{\sigma^2 + N\sigma_A^2} \cdot \frac{\mu_A}{\sigma_A^2} + \frac{N\sigma^2 \sigma_A^2}{\sigma^2 + N\sigma_A^2} \cdot \frac{\bar{x}}{\sigma^2}$$

**The Weighted Average Form:**
$$\mu_{A|\mathbf{x}} = \lambda \mu_A + (1 - \lambda) \bar{x}$$

Where the weight $\lambda$ is defined as:
$$\lambda = \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + N\sigma_A^2}$$

---

**Normalization and Sifting:**
Finally, we confirm the posterior is a valid PDF. Using the standard Gaussian integral property:
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2\sigma_{A|\mathbf{x}}^2} (A - \mu_{A|\mathbf{x}})^2 \right) dA = \sqrt{2\pi \sigma_{A|\mathbf{x}}^2}$$

Bayesian Estimate

The posterior distribution is Gaussian:

( p(A\mid X) \sim N(\mu_{A\mid X},\sigma^2_{A\mid X}) )

The Bayesian estimator is:

( \hat{A}=E[A\mid X] )

Thus:

( \hat{A}=\mu_{A\mid X}=\lambda \mu_A +(1-\lambda)\bar{X} )

where:

( \lambda=\frac{1}{1+N\sigma_A^2/\sigma^2} )

Special cases:

If:

( \lambda=1 )

then:

( \sigma_A^2\to 0 )

and the prior is very strong.

Hence:

( \hat{A}=\mu_A )

If:

( \lambda=0 )

then:

( \sigma_A^2\to \infty )

and:

( \hat{A}=\bar{X} )

Posterior variance:

( \sigma^2_{A\mid X}=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{\sigma_A^2}+\frac{N}{\sigma^2}} )

As:

( N\to\infty )

we get:

( \sigma^2_{A\mid X}\to 0 )

The figures illustrate:

• Effect of strong prior information.
• Shrinking posterior variance with increasing observations.
• Combination of prior density and likelihood.
• Posterior density centered between prior mean and sample evidence.

Limiting Cases of Bayesian Estimation

From the posterior mean:

( \mu_{A\mid X}=
\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+N\sigma_A^2}\mu_A
+
\frac{N\sigma_A^2}{\sigma^2+N\sigma_A^2}\bar{X} )

As:

( N\to\infty )

we obtain:

( \mu_{A\mid X}\to \bar{X} )

Thus with large number of observations, the estimator is dominated by the data.

Also:

( \lim_{\sigma_A^2\to\infty}\mu_{A\mid X} )

gives:

( \mu_{A\mid X}=\bar{X} )

Hence an uninformative prior leads to the sample mean estimator.

The figure illustrates posterior concentration as:

( \sigma_A^2\to\infty )

Validation: Prior Knowledge Improves Estimation Accuracy

The Bayesian estimator is:

( \hat{A}_{BMMSE}=E[A\mid X] )

The Bayesian mean square error is:

( BMSE=
\iint (A-\hat{A}(X))^2 p(A\mid X)p(X)\,dA\,dX )

Substituting:

( BMSE=
\int \left( \int (A-E[A\mid X])^2 p(A\mid X)\,dA \right)p(X)\,dX )

Thus:

( BMSE=
\int \sigma^2_{A\mid X} p(X)\,dX )

Since:

( \sigma^2_{A\mid X}=
\frac{1}{\frac{1}{\sigma_A^2}+\frac{N}{\sigma^2}} )

we get:

( BMSE=
\frac{1}{\frac{1}{\sigma_A^2}+\frac{N}{\sigma^2}} )

or equivalently:

( BMSE=
\frac{\sigma^2}{N}\cdot
\frac{1}{1+\frac{\sigma^2}{N\sigma_A^2}} )

Hence:

( BMSE<\frac{\sigma^2}{N} )

From the Bayesian mean square error expression:

( BMSE=
\frac{\sigma^2}{N}\cdot
\frac{1}{1+\frac{\sigma^2}{N\sigma_A^2}} )

Since:

( \frac{1}{1+\frac{\sigma^2}{N\sigma_A^2}}<1 )

we obtain:

( BMSE\leq \frac{\sigma^2}{N} )

which is lower than the classical CRB.

Hence estimation is improved using prior information.

Gaussian Filter

If:

( p(A) ) is Gaussian,

and:

( p(X\mid A) ) is Gaussian,

then the posterior distribution:

( p(A\mid X) )

is also Gaussian.

Thus Gaussian structure is preserved:

• Prior \rightarrow Gaussian
• Likelihood \rightarrow Gaussian
• Posterior \rightarrow Gaussian

Theorem

If:

( \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} )

is jointly Gaussian, then:

( p(y\mid x) )

is also Gaussian.

Conditional mean:

=E(y)+\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(x,y)}{\sigma_x^2}(x-E(x)) )

Conditional variance:

( \sigma^2_{y\mid x}
=\sigma_y^2-\frac{\mathrm{Cov}^2(x,y)}{\sigma_x^2} )

Correlation coefficient:

( \rho=
\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(x,y)}{\sqrt{\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2}} )

Using the correlation coefficient:

( \rho=
\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(x,y)}{\sigma_x\sigma_y} )

the conditional variance becomes:

( \sigma^2_{y\mid x}=\sigma_y^2(1-\rho^2) )

Proof Result

The conditional pdf is:

( p(y\mid x)=\frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)} )

For jointly Gaussian variables:

=\frac{1}{2\pi |C|^{1/2}}

Definition: Autocorrelation Sequence (ACS)

( k )

( r^*(k)
=\left[E\left(y(n)y^*(n-k)\right)\right]^* )

metadata.subject: MDA
metadata.title: Power Spectral Density of Random Signals

pages.text:
Continuing the autocorrelation properties:

( r^*(k)
=E[y(n-k)y^*(n)] )

Thus:

( r(k)=r^*(-k) )

Also:

( r(0)\geq |r(k)| )

for all:

( k )

Average power:

( r(0)=E[y(n)y^*(n)] )

Hence:

( r(0)=E[|y(n)|^2]\geq |r(k)| )

Define the covariance matrix:

( R_{m\times m} )

with entries:

( r(i-j) )

The matrix:

( R )

is positive semi-definite.

Definition: Power Spectral Density (PSD)

1.

( \Phi(\omega)
=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} r(k)e^{-j\omega k} )

which is the DTFT of the autocorrelation sequence.

Inverse relation:

( r(k)
=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\Phi(\omega)e^{j\omega k}d\omega )

At:

( k=0 )

( r(0)
=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\Phi(\omega)d\omega )

Thus:

( \Phi(\omega) )

represents the power spectral density.

2.

( \Phi(\omega)
=\lim_{N\to\infty}
E\left\{
\frac{1}{N}
\left|\sum y(n)e^{-j\omega n}\right|^2
\right\} )

Definition of PSD:

( \Phi(\omega)
=\lim_{N\to\infty}
E\left\{
\frac{1}{N}
\left|\sum y(n)e^{-j\omega n}\right|^2
\right\} )

If:

( \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}|k|r(k)=0 )

then the autocorrelation sequence decays rapidly.

Properties of PSD

1.

( \Phi(\omega)\geq 0 )

for all:

( \omega )

This follows from the PSD definition.

2.

( \Phi(\omega)
=r(0)+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\mathrm{Re}\{r(k)e^{-j\omega k}\} )

Starting from:

( \Phi(\omega)
=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}r(k)e^{-j\omega k} )

Separate positive and negative indices:

( \Phi(\omega)
=r(0)+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}r(k)e^{-j\omega k}
+\sum_{k=-\infty}^{-1}r(k)e^{-j\omega k} )

Using:

( r(-k)=r^*(k) )

we get:

( \Phi(\omega)
=r(0)+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}r(k)e^{-j\omega k}
+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}r^*(k)e^{j\omega k} )

Hence:

( \Phi(\omega)
=r(0)+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\mathrm{Re}\{r(k)e^{-j\omega k}\} )

If:

( r(k) )

is real, then:

( \Phi(\omega)
=r(0)+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}r(k)\cos(\omega k) )

Hence:

• The spectrum is symmetric about the vertical axis.
• The spectrum is even.

Linear Systems

Consider a linear system with transfer function:

( H(\omega) )

Input:

( x(n) )

with PSD:

( \Phi_x(\omega) )

Output:

( y(n) )

with PSD:

( \Phi_y(\omega) )

The transfer function is:

( H(\omega)=\sum_k h(k)e^{-j\omega k} )

where:

( h(k) )

is the impulse response.

The output sequence is:

( y(n)=\sum_k h(k)x(n-k) )

which is a linear convolution.

The output PSD is:

( \Phi_y(\omega)=|H(\omega)|^2\Phi_x(\omega) )

This is known as the power transfer relation.

The output autocorrelation is:

( r_y(m)=E[y(n)y^*(n-m)] )

Substituting:

( y(n)=\sum_k h(k)x(n-k) )

gives:

( r_y(m)
=E\left\{
\left(\sum_k h(k)x(n-k)\right)
\left(\sum_l h^*(l)x^*(n-m-l)\right)
\right\} )

Continuing the derivation of output PSD:

( r_y(m)
=E\left\{
\left(\sum_k h(k)x(n-k)\right)
\left(\sum_l h^*(l)x^*(n-m-l)\right)
\right\} )

Using linearity of expectation:

( r_y(m)
=\sum_k\sum_l h(k)h^*(l)
E[x(n-k)x^*(n-m-l)] )

Since:

( E[x(n-k)x^*(n-m-l)]
=r_x(m+k-l) )

we get:

( r_y(m)
=\sum_k\sum_l h(k)h^*(l)r_x(m+k-l) )

Taking DTFT:

( \Phi_y(\omega)
=\sum_m r_y(m)e^{-j\omega m} )

Substituting:

( \Phi_y(\omega)
=\sum_k\sum_l h(k)h^*(l)
\sum_m r_x(m+k-l)e^{-j\omega m} )

Using index substitution:

( p=m+k-l )

Thus:

( \Phi_y(\omega)
=\sum_k h(k)e^{j\omega k}
\sum_l h^*(l)e^{-j\omega l}
\sum_p r_x(p)e^{-j\omega p} )

Recognizing the DTFT terms:

( \Phi_y(\omega)
=H(\omega)H^*(\omega)\Phi_x(\omega) )

Therefore:

( \Phi_y(\omega)=|H(\omega)|^2\Phi_x(\omega) )

The output variance is:

( \sigma_y^2
=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|H(\omega)|^2\Phi_x(\omega)d\omega )

The figure illustrates variance reduction with increasing:

( N )

Reference Problem

Given:

( \{y(n)\} )

for:

( n=0,1,\ldots,N-1 )

Assume:

( y(n) )

is a second-order stationary sequence.

Estimate:

( \Phi(\omega) )

using:

( \hat{\Phi}(\omega) )

Non-parametric Methods

Periodogram:

( \hat{\Phi}(\omega)
=\frac{1}{N}
\left|\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}y(n)e^{-j\omega n}\right|^2 )

This is an estimator of:

( \Phi(\omega) )

The PSD definition is:

( \Phi(\omega)
=\lim_{N\to\infty}
E\left\{
\frac{1}{N}
\left|\sum y(n)e^{-j\omega n}\right|^2
\right\} )

Correlogram:

( \hat{\Phi}_c(\omega)
=\sum_{m=-(N-1)}^{N-1}\hat{r}(m)e^{-j\omega m} )

The estimated autocorrelation sequence is:

( \hat{r}(k) )

Unbiased estimator:

( \hat{r}(k)
=\frac{1}{N-|k|}
\sum_{n=0}^{N-|k|-1}y(n)y^*(n+k) )

for:

( 0\leq k\leq N-1 )

The estimator has high variance.

Biased estimator:

( \hat{r}(k)
=\frac{1}{N}
\sum y(n)y^*(n+k) )

for:

( 0\leq k\leq N-1 )

For many stationary signals:

( r(k) )

decays rapidly.

For large:

( k )

( r(k)\to 0 )

Hence:

( \hat{r}(N-1)
=\frac{1}{N-(N-1)}y(0)y^*(N-1)
= y(0)y^*(N-1) )

and:

( E[\hat{r}(N-1)]
=E[y(0)y^*(N-1)] )

Thus:

( \hat{r}(k) )

is an accurate estimator.

Also:

( \hat{r}(k) )

is positive semi-definite.

Therefore:

( \hat{\Phi}(\omega) )

and:

( \hat{\Phi}_c(\omega) )

are related.

Proof

Consider the signal:

( y(n) )

driven by white Gaussian noise.

Define:

( x(n)
=\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{k=1}^{N}y(k)e^{-j\omega k} )

Consider white Gaussian noise:

( e(n)\rightarrow H(\omega)\rightarrow y(n) )

The output PSD is:

( \Phi_y(\omega)=|H(\omega)|^2\Phi_e(\omega) )

If:

( e(n) )

is white noise, then:

( E[e(n)e^*(m)]=\delta(n-m) )

Hence:

( \Phi_e(\omega)=1 )

Therefore:

( \Phi_y(\omega)=|H(\omega)|^2 )

which is the periodogram.

Consider:

( r_x(k)=E[x(n)x^*(n-k)] )

where:

( x(n)
=\frac{1}{N}
\sum_r y(r)e^{-j\omega r}e^{j\omega n} )

Then:

( r_x(k)
=\frac{1}{N^2}
E\left\{
\sum_r\sum_s y(r)e^{-j\omega r}y^*(s)e^{j\omega s}
\right\} )

Using:

( E[y(r)y^*(s)]=\delta(r-s) )

we obtain:

( r_x(k)
=\frac{1}{N^2}
\sum_r y(r)e^{-j\omega r} )

Hence:

( r_x(k)
=\begin{cases}
\hat{\Phi}(\omega) & k=0 \\
0 & k\neq 0
\end{cases} )

The PSD becomes:

( \Phi_x(\omega)
=\sum_k r_x(k)e^{-j\omega k} )

Thus:

( \Phi_x(\omega)
=\sum_{k=-(N-1)}^{N-1}r_x(k)e^{-j\omega k}
=\hat{\Phi}_c(\omega) )

The periodogram estimator is:

( \hat{\Phi}(\omega)
=\frac{1}{N}
\left|\sum x(n)e^{-j\omega n}\right|^2 )

Implementation

The frequency variable:

( \omega )

is continuous and difficult to compute directly.

Frequency sampling:

( \omega_k=\frac{2\pi k}{N} )

for:

( k=0,1,\ldots,N-1 )

Thus:

( \Delta\omega=\frac{2\pi}{N} )

From sampling theory:

• More samples in time correspond to reduced frequency spacing.

The DFT is:

( Y(k)
=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}y(n)e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}kn} )

which can be computed using FFT.

Hence:

( \hat{\Phi}(k)
=\frac{1}{N}|Y(k)|^2 )

Zero Padding

Suppose:

( L>N )

Append:

( L-N )

zeros to the sequence.

Then:

( \hat{\Phi}(\omega_k)
\rightarrow
\omega_k=\frac{2\pi k}{L} )

for:

( 0\leq k\leq L-1 )

Thus:

( L\gg N )

corresponds to oversampling in frequency.

Zero padding increases frequency sampling density.

If:

( L\gg N )

then the spectrum becomes densely sampled.

Example

Given:

( y )

with:

( p(y\mid a)\sim N(a,\sigma^2) )

Find:

( p(a\mid y) )

using Bayes rule:

( p(a\mid y)=\frac{p(a)p(y\mid a)}{p(y)} )

where:

( p(y)=\int p(a)p(y\mid a)da )

Assume:

( a\rightarrow y(n) )

with:

( y(n)=a+w(n) )

and:

( w(n) )

is white Gaussian noise.

The likelihood is:

( p(y(n)\mid a)
=\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{1/2}}
\exp\left[-\frac{(y(n)-a)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right] )

For independent observations:

( p(y\mid a)
=\prod_{n=0}^{N-1}p(y(n)\mid a) )

The parameter:

( a )

acts as the mean of the Gaussian observations.

pages.text:
The posterior distribution is:

( p(a\mid y)
=\frac{p(y,a)}{p(y)} )

where:

( p(y,a) )

is the joint distribution.

The marginal distribution of:

( y )

is:

( p(y)
=\int p(y,a)da )

Thus:

( p(y) )

is obtained by integrating over the parameter:

( a )

The conditional distribution becomes:

( p(a\mid y)
=\frac{p(y,a)}{p(y)} )

The conditional expectation is:

( E[a\mid y]
=\int a\,p(a\mid y)da )

Interpretation:

• Multiplying:

( a\cdot p(a\mid y) )

and integrating gives the posterior mean.

• The posterior mean is a scalar quantity.

• The marginal density:

( p(y) )

is also scalar-valued.

Signals with Rational Spectra

The power spectral density is:

( \Phi(\omega)
=\frac{\sum_{k=0}^{P} b_ke^{-j\omega k}}{\sum_{k=0}^{Q} a_ke^{-j\omega k}} )

This corresponds to the spectral factorization theorem.

For continuous-time PSD:

( \Phi(\omega)=\left|\frac{B(\omega)}{A(\omega)}\right|^2 )

Consider the system:

( e(n)\rightarrow H(\omega)\rightarrow y(n) )

where:

( H(\omega)=\frac{B(\omega)}{A(\omega)} )

The output PSD is:

( \Phi_y(\omega)=|H(\omega)|^2\Phi_e(\omega) )

Assuming:

( \Phi_e(\omega)=\sigma_e^2 )

Define:

( A(\omega)=\sum_{k=0}^{Q} a_ke^{-j\omega k} )

and:

( B(\omega)=\sum_{k=0}^{P} b_ke^{-j\omega k} )

Then:

( |A(\omega)|^2=A(\omega)A^*(\omega) )

Expanding:

( r_0=\sum_i a_i^2 )

( r_1=\sum_i a_ia^*_{i+1} )

and in general:

( r_k=\sum_i a_ia^*_{i+k} )

Continuing the rational spectrum derivation:

( \sum_{i=0}^{Q}a_ie^{-j\omega i}
\sum_{m=0}^{Q}a_m^*e^{j\omega m} )

Hence:

( \Phi(\omega)
=\sigma_e^2
\frac{B(\omega)B^*(\omega)}{A(\omega)A^*(\omega)} )

in discrete time.

Also:

( \Phi(\omega)=\Phi(z)|_{z=e^{j\omega}} )

on the unit circle.

Poles occur in conjugate pairs.

The autocorrelation sequence is exponentially decaying.

Pole-zero interpretation:

• Poles close to:

( \Phi(\omega)\rightarrow \infty )

• Zeros imply:

( \Phi(\omega)\rightarrow 0 )

Signal Model

Notation:

( y(n)=\frac{B(z)}{A(z)}e(n) )

Equivalently:

( A(z)y(n)=B(z)e(n) )

where:

( z^{-1} )

represents the delay operator.

Also:

( e(n) )

is white noise.

1. ARMA: Autoregressive Moving Average

( A(z)y(n)=B(z)e(n) )

metadata.subject: MDA
metadata.title: Discrete-Time Rational Spectra and ARMA Model

pages.text:
For the ARMA model:

( A(z)y(n)=B(z)e(n) )

Expanding:

( y(n)+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i y(n-i)
=\sum_{j=0}^{Q}b_j e(n-j) )

where:

• ( y(n) ) is the output.
• ( e(n) ) is the input white noise.
• ( a_i,b_j ) are ARMA coefficients.

2. AR: Autoregressive Model

For:

( A(z)y(n)=e(n) )

we get:

( y(n)+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i y(n-i)=e(n) )

where:

( a_i )

are AR coefficients.

3. MA: Moving Average Model

( y(n)=B(z)e(n) )

Thus:

( y(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{Q}b_j e(n-j) )

Using the z-transform:

( y(z)+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i y(z)z^{-i}
=e(z)\sum_{j=0}^{Q}b_j z^{-j} )

Hence:

( y(z)\left[1+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i z^{-i}\right]
=e(z)\sum_{j=0}^{Q}b_j z^{-j} )

The transfer function becomes:

( \frac{Y(z)}{E(z)}
=\frac{\sum_{j=0}^{Q}b_j z^{-j}}{1+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i z^{-i}} )

Therefore:

( \frac{Y(z)}{E(z)}=\frac{B(z)}{A(z)} )

The transfer function is:

( H(z)=\frac{Y(z)}{E(z)} )

where:

( A(z)=1+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i z^{-i} )

Covariance Structure of ARMA Process

Consider the model:

( y(t)+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i y(t-i)
=\sum_{j=0}^{Q}b_j e(t-j) )

Multiply by:

( y^*(t-k) )

Taking expectation:

( E[y(t)y^*(t-k)]
+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i E[y(t-i)y^*(t-k)]
=\sum_{j=0}^{Q}b_j E[e(t-j)y^*(t-k)] )

Using autocorrelation notation:

( r(k)+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i r(k-i)
=\sum_{j=0}^{Q}b_j E[e(t-j)y^*(t-k)] )

Now:

( y(t)=H(z)e(t) )

Expanding:

( y(t)=\sum_i h_i e(t-i) )

Hence:

( E[e(t-j)y^*(t-k)] )

( =E\left[e(t-j)\sum_i h_i^* e^*(t-k-i)\right] )

( =\sum_i h_i^* E[e(t-j)e^*(t-k-i)] )

Using white-noise property:

( E[e(t-j)e^*(t-k-i)]
=\delta(k+i-j)\sigma_e^2 )

Using the white-noise property:

( E[e(t-j)e^*(t-k-i)]
=\delta(k+i-j)\sigma_e^2 )

Thus:

( \sum_i h_i^*\delta(k+i-j)\sigma_e^2
=\sigma_e^2 h^*_{j-k} )

Hence:

( r(k)+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i r(k-i)
=\sigma_e^2\sum_{j=0}^{Q}b_j h^*_{j-k} )

where:

( H(z)=\frac{B(z)}{A(z)} )

and:

( B(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{Q}b_j z^{-j} )

Since:

( h_k )

is the impulse response:

• Causal system implies:

( h_k=0,\quad k<0 )

For:

( k>Q )

we get:

( j-k<0 )

Hence:

( h^*_{j-k}=0 )

Therefore:

( r(k)+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i r(k-i)=0 )

for:

( k>Q )

Spectral Estimation using AR Model

For the AR process:

( A(z)y(t)=e(t) )

or:

( y(t)+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i y(t-i)=e(t) )

Taking z-transform:

( Y(z)=\frac{E(z)}{1+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i z^{-i}} )

Thus the system behaves as an all-pole filter.

metadata.title: ARMA Covariance Relations and AR Spectral Model

pages.text:
For the AR process:

( Y(z)=\frac{E(z)}{1+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i z^{-i}} )

Thus the system is an all-pole filter.

The PSD exhibits narrow-band peaks near the pole locations.

Parameter estimation leads to a system of linear equations.

AR Model

Using the Yule-Walker equations:

( r(k)+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i r(k-i)
=\sigma_e^2\sum_{j=0}^{Q}b_j h^*_{j-k} )

For the AR case:

( b_0=1 )

Hence:

( r(0)+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i r(-i)=\sigma_e^2 )

and:

( r(1)+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i r(1-i)=0 )

( r(2)+\sum_{i=1}^{P}a_i r(2-i)=0 )

Continuing:

( r(P)+a_1r(P-1)+\cdots+a_Pr(0)=0 )

This gives the matrix equation:

( \begin{bmatrix}
r(0) & r(-1) & r(-2) & \cdots & r(-P+1) \\
r(1) & r(0) & r(-1) & \cdots & r(-P+2) \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\
r(P-1) & r(P-2) & \cdots & & r(0)
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
a_1 \\
a_2 \\
\vdots \\
a_P
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
-r(1) \\
-r(2) \\
\vdots \\
-r(P)
\end{bmatrix} )

The Yule-Walker equations can be written as:

( r_p+R_p\theta=0 )

where:

( r_p=
\begin{bmatrix}
r(1) \\
r(2) \\
\vdots \\
r(P)
\end{bmatrix} )

and:

( R_p=
\begin{bmatrix}
r(0) & r(1) & \cdots & r(P-1) \\
r(1) & r(0) & \cdots & r(P-2) \\
\vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\
r(P-1) & r(P-2) & \cdots & r(0)
\end{bmatrix} ) )

The parameter vector is:

( \theta=
\begin{bmatrix}
a_1 \\
a_2 \\
\vdots \\
a_P
\end{bmatrix} )

Hence the AR parameter estimate is:

( \hat{\theta}=-R_p^{-1}r_p )

which is the Yule-Walker solution.
